title: Microbes Eat Your Poop at the Sewage Plant #shorts
summary: At a treatment plant, air is pumped into tanks so oxygen-loving microbes eat the organic matter; this biological step removes about 85% of it (EPA). New York's plants take about 8-10 hours, and chlorine kills more than 99% of harmful bacteria.
sources: Screening removes large floating objects such as rags and sticks that might clog pipes or damage equipment; in a grit chamber cinders, sand and small stones settle; secondary (biological) treatment removes about 85 percent of the organic matter in sewage; done properly, chlorination kills more than 99 percent of the harmful bacteria in an effluent (US EPA, Wastewater Treatment Works... The Basics, EPA 833-F-98-002, May 1998): https://www3.epa.gov/npdes/pubs/bastre.pdf

NYC treatment: bar screens; primary settling tanks where the flow slows down and heavier sludge settles; air added so oxygen-loving microorganisms consume much of the organic material; final settling; disinfection with sodium hypochlorite, the same chemical found in household bleach; after about 8-10 hours the facilities release clean water; digesters heated to about 98°F for about 15 days, where microorganisms convert much of the material into biogas, which can produce heat and electricity for the facilities (NYC DEP, Wastewater Treatment System): https://www.nyc.gov/site/dep/water/wastewater-treatment-process.page

scenes.narration: At a sewage plant, about {85%|eighty-five percent} of the organic matter gets eaten.
Big tanks get pumped full of air, and oxygen-loving microbes eat the organic matter.
In New York, the whole cleanup takes about {8–10|eight to ten} hours.
Then chlorine kills more than {99%|ninety-nine percent} of the harmful bacteria.
So the real cleanup crew is tiny. And hungry.
